correctness.rationale: Block multiplication gives \(u_i v_j-u_j v_i=0\) and a free \(rst\)-dimensional central factor. An elementary tensor-rigidity lemma proves union of the two coordinate subspaces and rank-one determinantal variety. Over algebraic closure these are precisely three geometrically irreducible, noncontained components for \(r,s,t\ge2\). Dimension calculation, unique \((2,2,3)\) equidimensional solution and disjoint finite-field counting by mixed projective lines are proved for all parameters. Nine complete small finite-field enumerations corroborate every branch, including characteristic two and a nonprime field.

originality.rationale: The primary predecessor Goodwin–Röhrle (2012), Remark 3.1, states a two-component boundary parabolic case with block sizes \((1,1,m)\), not the all-arity \((r,1,s)\) geometry for r,s at least two. The new claim identifies three noncontained components, a unique equidimensional parameter, and complete finite-field tuple counts. Other inspected sources treat whole parabolic Lie algebras, their nilpotent cones, parabolic orbit problems, or different Lie algebras. The closest relevant public mathematical-record hits lack an implication to the exact three-block claim. An unknown equivalent elementary or determinantal treatment remains a priority risk.
residual_risks: An earlier general theorem on rank-one tensor commutator equations or parabolic nilradicals may subsume the three-component result without repeating its parameter notation.

General comprehensive literature coverage and independent mathematical audit are not established.

value.rationale: The Goodwin–Röhrle two-component boundary for block sizes \((1,1,m)\) motivates the first genuinely two-sided large-endblock case. Exactly three geometric components, their differing dimensions, one sharp equidimensional exception, and a complete higher-tuple finite-field enumeration give natural, nontrivial geometric and arithmetic invariants of an infinite three-parameter family. The result is more than a restatement of a general determinantal lemma.
